case_studies.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
case_studies.abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.
case_studies.summary: ReTrace turns natural‑language SOPs and logged LLM runs into code‑driven workflows that pick the next step automatically, cutting cost and latency while keeping accuracy close to the original LLM agent. The tool learns conditions from agent reasoning, compiles a rule document, and outputs an executable workflow for any orchestration platform. It achieved about 94% completion on 79 production SOPs at 24% lower cost, and ran 1.3 s versus 170 s for the agent on benchmark tests.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Export your SOP logs and the natural‑language SOPs; 2) Run ReTrace to generate rule‑based workflows; 3) Deploy the generated workflows in your orchestration platform (e.g., Airflow, Step Functions) to replace LLM calls, saving cost and reducing latency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: ReTrace addresses business process automation by converting LLM agent logs into reusable, low‑latency workflows, directly impacting IT engineers who build and maintain SOP orchestration. The approach is demonstrated on real production data, with open‑source code and runnable workflows, indicating practical maturity. The methodology is actionable: engineers could implement ReTrace in their own LLM‑driven pipelines or offer workflow conversion as a service, offering clear monetisation within 90 days. However, adoption requires integration with existing orchestration platforms, so the monetisation score is not maximum. Overall, the paper scores well across all criteria.

case_studies.title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
case_studies.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.
case_studies.summary: REAL is a new training loss that improves how speculative decoding models decide which draft tokens to keep, cutting inference time. By adjusting the training objective, the authors show that a Qwen model with a Domino drafter runs faster on a variety of tasks, with no change to the model code or inference pipeline. This could let you squeeze more speed out of your LLMs with a simple loss tweak.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference, you can try the REAL loss by re‑training your draft models: step 1, replace your current cross‑entropy loss with the REAL implementation from the provided GitHub repo; step 2, fine‑tune the draft model on your data; step 3, deploy the new model and measure acceptance length – you should see faster inference without altering the drafter architecture.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The REAL loss targets speculative decoding, a technique directly relevant to speeding up LLM inference on cloud platforms. It offers a practical improvement that can reduce compute costs for SaaS LLM services, making it immediately useful for IT engineers managing cloud-based LLM deployments. The paper provides released code and demonstrates performance gains in controlled experiments, indicating a mature, usable system. The improvement can be monetised quickly by reducing inference latency or cost, enabling IT teams to sell faster or cheaper LLM APIs within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
case_studies.abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how different LLM‑based evaluation methods reliably spot failures in complex agent workflows, proving that a mix of trace‑based checks and security red‑team tests uncovers hidden bugs that regular testing misses. It builds and compares three evaluation frameworks on two analytics agents, finding trace‑based methods give the best precision while red‑team tests find unique security issues.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, run a trace‑based LLM evaluation on your agents first to catch functional bugs, then add a red‑team LLM review for security gaps. Check that your orchestration logs are detailed enough for trace‑based checks. Ensure your CI pipeline stores execution traces for these evaluations.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses evaluation frameworks for LLM-based analytics agents, which is relevant to enterprise software engineering and DevOps. However, it is an academic comparison study without released code or a production system, so maturity is moderate. The concepts could be sold as a consulting service or integrated into existing QA pipelines within a few weeks, earning a modest monetisation score.

case_studies.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
case_studies.summary: Memory in LLM agents can cause mistakes by following bad lessons, and this paper introduces WikiTrace, a system that links each lesson to its original evidence so agents can verify and correct them. The result is better performance and less error on new tasks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a technique for improving LLM agent memory, which has limited direct applicability to day‑to‑day IT infrastructure work. The system is released with code, indicating a usable implementation, but the specific value proposition for IT engineers, such as endpoint or cloud management, is weak. No clear commercial or service use case emerges within a 90‑day window. Overall, the work has some relevance but offers limited immediate impact, maturity, or monetisation potential for the target audience.

case_studies.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
case_studies.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.
case_studies.summary: FERN is a table‑retrieval system for Text‑to‑SQL that uses pre‑trained retrievers and a LightGBM ranker to reorder 100 candidates, achieving near‑state‑of‑the‑art recall on several benchmark datasets without relying on large language models. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the correct database tables for a natural language query, which is crucial for accurate SQL generation. The system delivers high recall (up to 98% on Spider) and fast latency (≈208 ms per query).
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud database services, consider integrating a frozen retriever + LightGBM ranker pipeline like FERN to improve table recall in your Text‑to‑SQL application: 1) deploy a lightweight retriever ensemble (e.g., BM25, dense vector, and keyword matcher) to generate a 100‑candidate set; 2) extract up to 120 descriptive features per candidate (size, column names, statistics); 3) train a LightGBM ranker on a representative dataset (e.g., Spider training questions) and use it to re‑rank candidates at runtime, targeting a recall of 95%+ for top‑5 results.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes an improved table retrieval pipeline for text-to-SQL, but its applicability is narrow to database query systems and lacks a ready‑to‑deploy service. It is a research prototype with released code, but not a turnkey solution for infrastructure teams.
